description: I am in 1st grade. This is my first experience to participate in a challenge. I am excited to present my work.
summary:
We built Pale Blue Dot, a free, playable web app that tells the story of Voyager 1 for young kids (ages 6–8).

What we developed: an interactive journey — watch Voyager lift off, send a radio signal across the real distance and wait for its reply through the Deep Space Network, build the spacecraft part by part, open the Golden Record, and earn mission badges — all from real NASA facts, with sources.

How it addresses the challenge: Voyager 1 is humanity's farthest traveller — launched in 1977, now almost one light-day from Earth, and easy to forget. Our app keeps it abandoned but not forgotten, turning a faraway machine kids can't picture into a story they can play and remember.

Why it matters: I, Daibik, first learned about Voyager-1 at his first ASKC(Astronomical Society of Kansas City) event this year and wanted to share that wonder. Voyager-1 still works after nearly 50 years and carries our hello to the stars — its story belongs to the next generation of explorers.

Try it live: https://pale-blue-dot-980635685005.us-central1.run.app
details:
What it does / how it works

Pale Blue Dot is a free web app that turns the true story of Voyager 1 into a playable journey for young children (ages 6–8). Kids count down and watch the spacecraft lift off, transmit a radio message and wait for its reply across the real ~171-AU distance through NASA's Deep Space Network, build Voyager part by part, open the Golden Record, follow the mission timeline, and earn badges in a quiz academy. Every page is built from real NASA/JPL facts with sources shown, and a read-aloud button narrates the text for children who can't read yet.

Benefits and intended impact

Voyager 1 is humanity's farthest traveller — almost one light-day away and easy to forget. We wanted to keep it "abandoned but not forgotten" by turning a faraway machine into something a child can picture, play with, and remember. It is free, needs no login, and works on any phone, tablet or computer, so any family, classroom or science club can use it. Our hope is to spark the next generation's curiosity the way a first ASKC event sparked Daibik's.

Benefits and intended impact

Voyager 1 is humanity's farthest traveller — almost one light-day away and easy to forget. We wanted to keep it "abandoned but not forgotten" by turning a faraway machine into something a child can picture, play with, and remember. It is free, needs no login, and works on any phone, tablet or computer, so any family, classroom or science club can use it. Our hope is to spark the next generation's curiosity the way a first ASKC event sparked Daibik's.

Tools and technology

The web app is built with React 19, Vite 6 and TypeScript; a small Express 5 (TypeScript) backend uses Zod validation and privacy-first, anonymous analytics. The he signal animations are all hand-drawn as inline SVG with CSS keyframes — no stock art for the interactive parts. Sound effects use the Web Audio API and narration uses the browser's built-in Speech installing. It is deployed on Google Cloud Run (US region) and is fully open-source on GitHub.

How it's creative and what we considered

We turned learning into play. Instead of reading facts, children follow a guided explorer flow — chapter by chapter from launch to interstellar space — and do the science themselves: count down a launch, send a real-distance signal, and build Voyager piece by piece. Mission Academy then rewards what they learned with a friendly quiz and collectible explorer badges, and at the end each child designs a personalized take-home card they can print and keep — turning a lesson into a souvenir and a reason to come back. We designed for very young, non-reading users first (big visuals, read-aloud narration, gentle language) while keeping every fact accurate and sourced, and we balanced wonder with truth and cost with reach, so the app stays free and runs anywhere.
